If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $x$-component of $F=⟨4{x}^{3}+3{y}^{2}+2z,\,0,\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $x$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the front and back sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14068126/assets/4fd228a9bf0a2d8382139d3f804ee7c9b3fd8721c8ad079de43e61b9e8947240.png)

  

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the front surface. On this surface, we have $x=1$ for $0\le y\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=1$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨4{x}^{3}+3{y}^{2}+2z,\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨4+3{y}^{2}+2z,\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =4+3{y}^{2}+2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}4+3{y}^{2}+2z\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}4+3{y}^{2}+2z\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}4+3{y}^{2}+2z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[(4+2z)y+{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}4+2z+1\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2z+5\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[{z}^{2}+5z]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =9+15 \\  & =24\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the back surface. On this surface, we have $x=0$ for $0\le y\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 3.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨4{x}^{3}+3{y}^{2}+2z,\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨3{y}^{2}+2z,\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =-(3{y}^{2}+2z).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-(3{y}^{2}+2z)\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}3{y}^{2}+2z\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}3{y}^{2}+2z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{[{y}^{3}+2yz]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}1+2z\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{[z+{z}^{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-(3+9) \\  & =-12\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =24+(-12) \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$
